strings.b-00-meta.title: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
strings.b-00-meta.objectives.0: After this lesson you can describe the parts of the human eye and explain what each part does as light travels into it.
strings.b-00-meta.objectives.1: After this lesson you can explain accommodation and state the near point and the far point of a normal eye.
strings.b-00-meta.objectives.2: After this lesson you can identify myopia, hypermetropia and presbyopia and say which lens corrects each defect.
strings.b-00-meta.objectives.3: After this lesson you can explain refraction through a prism, dispersion and the rainbow, why stars twinkle, and why the sky is blue.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.0.definition: The thin transparent membrane forming the bulge on the front of the eyeball; most of the refraction of light entering the eye happens at its outer surface.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.1.definition: The dark muscular diaphragm behind the cornea that controls the size of the pupil.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.2.definition: The opening at the centre of the iris; it regulates and controls the amount of light entering the eye.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.3.definition: The light-sensitive screen at the back of the eye on which the eye lens forms an inverted real image.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.4.definition: The ability of the eye lens to adjust its focal length, done by changing its curvature with the ciliary muscles.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.5.definition: The least distance of distinct vision: the closest distance at which an object can be seen most distinctly without strain, about 25 cm for a normal young adult.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.6.definition: The farthest distance up to which the eye can see objects clearly; infinity for a normal eye.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.7.definition: Near-sightedness: nearby objects are clear but distant ones are not, because the image of a distant object forms in front of the retina; corrected by a concave lens.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.8.definition: Far-sightedness: distant objects are clear but nearby ones are not, because the image of a nearby object forms behind the retina; corrected by a convex lens.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.9.definition: The defect in which the near point recedes with ageing because the ciliary muscles weaken and the eye lens loses flexibility.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.10.definition: The splitting of white light into its seven component colours by a prism.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.11.definition: The band of coloured components of a light beam, in the order violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.12.definition: The angle at which a prism makes the emergent ray bend away from the direction of the incident ray.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.13.definition: The scattering of light by colloidal particles, which makes the path of the beam visible.
strings.b-01.paragraphs.0: Of all our sense organs, the eye is the one that lets us see the world and its colours. Close your eyes and you can still recognise many things by smell, taste, sound or touch, but you cannot tell what colour anything is.
strings.b-01.paragraphs.1: The human eye works very much like a camera. Its lens system forms an image on a light-sensitive screen inside the eye, and that screen is a membrane called the retina.
strings.b-01.paragraphs.2: The eyeball is roughly spherical, with a diameter of about 2.3 cm. Light enters it through a thin membrane at the front called the cornea, which forms a transparent bulge on the front surface of the eyeball.
strings.b-02.caption: The human eye. Light enters through the cornea and the pupil; the eye lens forms an inverted real image on the retina, and the optic nerve carries the signals to the brain.
strings.b-03.paragraphs.0: Most of the refraction of the light entering the eye happens at the outer surface of the cornea. The crystalline lens inside the eye only makes the finer adjustment of focal length needed to focus objects at different distances on the retina.
strings.b-03.paragraphs.1: Behind the cornea sits the iris, a dark muscular diaphragm. It controls the size of the pupil, the opening at its centre, and the pupil regulates and controls the amount of light entering the eye.
strings.b-03.paragraphs.2: At the back of the eye, the retina is a delicate membrane packed with an enormous number of light-sensitive cells. When light falls on them they get activated and generate electrical signals.
strings.b-03.paragraphs.3: These signals travel along the optic nerves to the brain. The brain interprets them and processes the information, so that we perceive objects as they are.
strings.b-03.paragraphs.4: The eye lens forms an inverted real image of the object on the retina. It is the brain that makes sense of this image for us.
strings.b-04.question: The human eye forms the image of an object at its
strings.b-04.explanation: The eye is like a camera: its lens system forms an image on the light-sensitive screen at the back of the eye, and that screen is the retina.
strings.b-05.question: Where does most of the refraction of light entering the human eye take place?
strings.b-05.options.0: at the outer surface of the cornea
strings.b-05.explanation: Most of the refraction happens at the outer surface of the cornea. The crystalline lens only provides the finer adjustment of focal length needed to focus objects at different distances on the retina.
strings.b-06.paragraphs.0: The eye lens is made of a fibrous, jelly-like material. Its curvature can be changed to some extent by the ciliary muscles, and changing the curvature changes the focal length of the lens.
strings.b-06.paragraphs.1: When the ciliary muscles are relaxed, the lens becomes thin. Its focal length increases, and this lets us see distant objects clearly.
strings.b-06.paragraphs.2: When you look at an object closer to the eye, the ciliary muscles contract. The curvature of the eye lens increases, the lens becomes thicker, and its focal length decreases. This lets us see nearby objects clearly.
strings.b-06.paragraphs.3: The ability of the eye lens to adjust its focal length is called accommodation.
strings.b-07.paragraphs.0: There is a limit to accommodation. The focal length of the eye lens cannot be decreased below a certain minimum. Try reading a printed page held very close to your eyes: the image blurs and the eye feels strained.
strings.b-07.paragraphs.1: To see an object comfortably and distinctly, hold it about 25 cm from the eyes. The minimum distance at which objects can be seen most distinctly without strain is called the least distance of distinct vision, or the near point of the eye. For a young adult with normal vision the near point is about 25 cm.
strings.b-07.paragraphs.2: The farthest point up to which the eye can see objects clearly is called the far point of the eye. For a normal eye the far point is infinity. So a normal eye can see clearly objects that are anywhere between 25 cm and infinity.
strings.b-07.paragraphs.3: Sometimes the crystalline lens of people at old age becomes milky and cloudy. This condition is called cataract. It causes partial or complete loss of vision, and vision can be restored through a cataract surgery.
strings.b-08.question: What is meant by the power of accommodation of the eye?
strings.b-08.options.0: The ability of the eye to change the size of its pupil
strings.b-08.options.1: The ability of the eye lens to adjust its focal length
strings.b-08.options.2: The ability of the retina to change its sensitivity
strings.b-08.options.3: The ability of the eye to move inside its socket
strings.b-08.explanation: Accommodation is the ability of the eye lens to adjust its focal length, so that objects at different distances are focussed on the retina. The ciliary muscles do the adjusting by changing the curvature of the lens.
strings.b-09.question: The human eye can focus on objects at different distances by adjusting the focal length of the eye lens. This is due to
strings.b-09.explanation: Adjusting the focal length of the eye lens is exactly what accommodation means. Presbyopia, myopia and hypermetropia are defects, not the normal ability.
strings.b-10.question: The change in focal length of an eye lens is caused by the action of the
strings.b-10.explanation: The ciliary muscles change the curvature of the eye lens. More curvature means a thicker lens and a shorter focal length; relaxed muscles mean a thin lens and a longer focal length.
strings.b-11.question: The least distance of distinct vision for a young adult with normal vision is about
strings.b-11.explanation: The near point, or least distance of distinct vision, is about 25 cm for a young adult with normal vision.
strings.b-12.question: What are the far point and the near point of a human eye with normal vision?
strings.b-12.options.0: Far point 25 cm, near point infinity
strings.b-12.options.1: Far point infinity, near point 25 cm
strings.b-12.options.2: Far point 2.5 cm, near point infinity
strings.b-12.options.3: Far point infinity, near point 2.3 cm
strings.b-12.explanation: For a normal eye the far point is infinity and the near point is about 25 cm, so the eye can see clearly anything between 25 cm and infinity.
strings.b-13.question: Why is a normal eye not able to see clearly the objects placed closer than 25 cm?
strings.b-13.options.0: The pupil cannot open wide enough
strings.b-13.options.1: The focal length of the eye lens cannot be decreased below a certain minimum limit
strings.b-13.options.2: The retina stops sending electrical signals
strings.b-13.options.3: The iris blocks the light completely
strings.b-13.explanation: The ciliary muscles can increase the curvature of the eye lens only up to a point, so the focal length cannot be reduced below a minimum. Objects closer than about 25 cm therefore give a blurred image and strain the eye.
strings.b-14.question: What happens to the image distance in the eye when we increase the distance of an object from the eye?
strings.b-14.options.2: It stays the same, because the image is always formed on the retina
strings.b-14.explanation: The retina is fixed at the back of the eye, so the image must always fall on it. When the object moves farther away, the eye does not move the image; instead the ciliary muscles change the curvature of the eye lens and hence its focal length, so that the image still lands on the retina.
strings.b-15.paragraphs.0: Sometimes the eye gradually loses its power of accommodation. The person then cannot see objects distinctly and comfortably, and vision becomes blurred because of refractive defects of the eye.
strings.b-15.paragraphs.1: There are mainly three common refractive defects of vision: myopia or near-sightedness, hypermetropia or far-sightedness, and presbyopia. They can be corrected by using suitable spherical lenses.
strings.b-16.paragraphs.0: Myopia is also known as near-sightedness. A person with myopia can see nearby objects clearly but cannot see distant objects distinctly. The far point of such a person is nearer than infinity; the person may see clearly only up to a distance of a few metres.
strings.b-16.paragraphs.1: In a myopic eye, the image of a distant object is formed in front of the retina and not at the retina itself. This defect may arise because of excessive curvature of the eye lens, or because the eyeball has become elongated.
strings.b-16.paragraphs.2: Myopia is corrected by using a concave lens of suitable power. The concave lens brings the image back on to the retina.
strings.b-17.caption: Myopia and its correction. In the myopic eye (left) the parallel rays from a distant object meet at the point F in front of the retina. A concave lens of suitable power (right) spreads the rays slightly before they enter the eye, so the eye lens brings them together exactly on the retina.
strings.b-18.paragraphs.0: Hypermetropia is also known as far-sightedness. A person with hypermetropia can see distant objects clearly but cannot see nearby objects distinctly. The near point of such a person is farther away than the normal 25 cm, so the person has to keep reading material much beyond 25 cm from the eye.
strings.b-18.paragraphs.1: This happens because light rays from a close by object are focussed at a point behind the retina. The defect arises either because the focal length of the eye lens is too long, or because the eyeball has become too small.
strings.b-18.paragraphs.2: Hypermetropia is corrected by using a convex lens of appropriate power. Eye-glasses with converging lenses provide the additional focussing power needed to form the image on the retina.
strings.b-19.caption: Hypermetropia and its correction. In the hypermetropic eye (left) the rays from a nearby object would meet at the point F behind the retina. A convex lens of appropriate power (right) adds the extra converging power, so the rays meet on the retina.
strings.b-20.paragraphs.0: The power of accommodation of the eye usually decreases with ageing, and the near point gradually recedes. People then find it difficult to see nearby objects comfortably and distinctly without corrective eye-glasses. This defect is called presbyopia. It arises due to the gradual weakening of the ciliary muscles and diminishing flexibility of the eye lens.
strings.b-20.paragraphs.1: Sometimes a person may suffer from both myopia and hypermetropia. Such people often require bi-focal lenses, which consist of both concave and convex lenses: the upper portion is a concave lens for distant vision, and the lower part is a convex lens for near vision.
strings.b-20.paragraphs.2: These days refractive defects can also be corrected with contact lenses or through surgical interventions.
strings.b-21.question: A person with a myopic eye cannot see objects beyond 1.2 m distinctly. What should be the type of the corrective lens used to restore proper vision?
strings.b-21.explanation: Myopia is corrected by a concave lens of suitable power. The person's far point is only 1.2 m, so the concave lens must bring the image of a distant object back from in front of the retina on to the retina.
strings.b-22.question: A student has difficulty reading the blackboard while sitting in the last row. What could be the defect the child is suffering from, and how can it be corrected?
strings.b-22.options.0: Hypermetropia, corrected by a convex lens
strings.b-22.options.1: Myopia, corrected by a concave lens
strings.b-22.options.2: Presbyopia, corrected by a bi-focal lens
strings.b-22.explanation: The blackboard is far away, and a child who cannot read it from the last row cannot see distant objects distinctly. That is myopia, and it is corrected with a concave lens of suitable power.
strings.b-23.title: Lens power and focal length
strings.b-23.steps.0.title: Power is measured in dioptres
strings.b-23.steps.0.detail: Lens power is quoted in dioptres, written D. The numerical problems in this chapter use values such as -5.5 D for distant vision and +1.5 D for near vision.
strings.b-23.steps.1.title: Power and focal length
strings.b-23.steps.1.detail: The power P of a lens and its focal length f in metres are related by P = 1/f, so f = 1/P. Work with f in metres and the power comes out in dioptres.
strings.b-23.steps.2.title: The sign of the power tells you which lens
strings.b-23.steps.2.detail: The lens used to correct myopia, which is a concave lens, is the one the chapter quotes with a minus sign (-5.5 D). The lens used to correct hypermetropia, which is a convex lens, is the one quoted with a plus sign (+1.5 D).
strings.b-24.problem: A person needs a lens of power -5.5 dioptres for correcting his distant vision. For correcting his near vision he needs a lens of power +1.5 dioptre. What is the focal length of the lens required for correcting (i) distant vision, and (ii) near vision?
strings.b-24.steps.0.title: Write down what is given
strings.b-24.steps.0.detail: Power of the lens for distant vision P = -5.5 D. Power of the lens for near vision P = +1.5 D.
strings.b-24.steps.1.title: Choose the relation
strings.b-24.steps.1.detail: Power and focal length are related by P = 1/f with f in metres, so f = 1/P. The answer comes out in metres.
strings.b-24.steps.2.title: Distant vision
strings.b-24.steps.2.detail: f = 1/(-5.5) = -0.18 m, that is about -18 cm. The negative sign shows it is a concave lens.
strings.b-24.steps.3.title: Near vision
strings.b-24.steps.3.detail: f = 1/(+1.5) = +0.67 m, that is about +67 cm. The positive sign shows it is a convex lens.
strings.b-24.answer: Distant vision: focal length about -0.18 m (about -18 cm), a concave lens. Near vision: focal length about +0.67 m (about +67 cm), a convex lens.
strings.b-25.problem: The far point of a myopic person is 80 cm in front of the eye. What is the nature and power of the lens required to correct the problem?
strings.b-25.steps.0.title: What the lens has to do
strings.b-25.steps.0.detail: The person must be able to see distant objects clearly. The corrective lens must therefore form the image of a very distant object at the person's own far point, 80 cm in front of the eye.
strings.b-25.steps.1.title: Focal length of the required lens
strings.b-25.steps.1.detail: For an object at infinity the image forms at the focal point of the lens, so the focal length must be 80 cm: f = -80 cm = -0.8 m. The minus sign is used because this image is on the same side of the lens as the object.
strings.b-25.steps.2.title: Power of the lens
strings.b-25.steps.3.title: Nature of the lens
strings.b-25.steps.3.detail: A negative power means a concave lens, which is exactly what myopia needs.
strings.b-25.answer: A concave lens of power -1.25 D.
strings.b-26.problem: Make a diagram to show how hypermetropia is corrected. The near point of a hypermetropic eye is 1 m. What is the power of the lens required to correct this defect? Assume that the near point of the normal eye is 25 cm.
strings.b-26.steps.0.title: What the lens has to do
strings.b-26.steps.0.detail: The person must be able to read at the normal near point of 25 cm. So an object placed at 25 cm must produce an image at the person's own near point, 1 m, on the same side of the lens.
strings.b-26.steps.1.title: Object distance
strings.b-26.steps.1.detail: u = -25 cm = -0.25 m. The object is on the near side of the lens, so its distance is taken as negative.
strings.b-26.steps.2.title: Image distance
strings.b-26.steps.2.detail: v = -1 m. The image is virtual and on the same side as the object, so it is also negative.
strings.b-26.steps.3.title: Apply the lens formula
strings.b-26.steps.4.title: Focal length and power
strings.b-26.steps.4.detail: f = 1/3 m = +0.33 m, and P = 1/f = +3.0 D. The positive sign tells us the lens is convex.
strings.b-26.answer: A convex lens of power +3.0 D (focal length about +0.33 m). The ray diagram is the one shown in the figure above: the convex lens makes the rays from the object at 25 cm meet on the retina.
strings.b-27.paragraphs.0: Light passing through a rectangular glass slab comes out parallel to the direction in which it entered, only slightly displaced sideways, because the slab's two refracting surfaces are parallel.
strings.b-27.paragraphs.1: A triangular glass prism is different. It has two triangular bases and three rectangular lateral surfaces, and these surfaces are inclined to each other. The angle between its two lateral faces is called the angle of the prism.
strings.b-27.paragraphs.2: When a ray of light PE falls on one refracting face of the prism, it bends towards the normal as it enters the glass and travels inside as the refracted ray EF. At the second face it passes from glass to air, so it bends away from the normal and leaves as the emergent ray FS.
strings.b-27.paragraphs.3: The peculiar shape of the prism makes the emergent ray bend at an angle to the direction of the incident ray. This angle is called the angle of deviation.
strings.b-28.caption: Refraction of light through a triangular glass prism. PE is the incident ray, EF the refracted ray and FS the emergent ray. The angle of incidence is i, the angle of refraction is r, the angle of emergence is e, the angle of the prism is A, and D is the angle of deviation between the extended incident ray (dashed) and the emergent ray.
strings.b-29.question: In a triangular glass prism, the angle between its two lateral faces is called
strings.b-29.explanation: A triangular prism has two triangular bases and three rectangular lateral surfaces. The angle between its two lateral faces is the angle of the prism, marked A in the ray diagram.
strings.b-30.paragraphs.0: When a narrow beam of white light from the Sun is allowed to fall on a glass prism and the emerging light is caught on a nearby screen, a beautiful band of colours appears. The prism has split the white light into a band of colours.
strings.b-30.paragraphs.1: The colours you see, in order, are violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red. The acronym VIBGYOR helps you remember the sequence.
strings.b-30.paragraphs.2: The band of the coloured components of a light beam is called its spectrum. The splitting of light into its component colours is called dispersion.
strings.b-30.paragraphs.3: Why do we get these colours? Different colours of light bend through different angles with respect to the incident ray as they pass through a prism. Red light bends the least and violet bends the most. So the rays of each colour emerge along different paths and become distinct.
strings.b-31.caption: Dispersion of white light by a glass prism. The beam of white light is split into its seven components, which reach the screen as the spectrum: red (R) is deviated least and violet (V) the most, so the order from top to bottom is R, O, Y, G, B, I, V.
strings.b-32.paragraphs.0: Isaac Newton was the first to use a glass prism to obtain the spectrum of sunlight. When he tried to split the colours further with another similar prism, he could not get any more colours. When he placed a second identical prism in an inverted position, all the colours passed through it and a beam of white light emerged on the other side. This gave Newton the idea that sunlight is made up of seven colours.
strings.b-32.paragraphs.1: Any light that gives a spectrum similar to that of sunlight is often referred to as white light.
strings.b-32.paragraphs.2: A rainbow is a natural spectrum appearing in the sky after a rain shower. It is caused by dispersion of sunlight by the tiny water droplets present in the atmosphere. A rainbow is always formed in a direction opposite to that of the Sun.
strings.b-32.paragraphs.3: The water droplets act like small prisms. They refract and disperse the incident sunlight, then reflect it internally, and finally refract it again as it comes out of the raindrop. Because of this dispersion and internal reflection, different colours reach the observer's eye.
strings.b-32.paragraphs.4: You can also see a rainbow on a sunny day by looking at the sky through a waterfall or a water fountain with the Sun behind you.
strings.b-33.question: When white light passes through a glass prism, which colour bends the most and which the least?
strings.b-33.options.0: Red bends the most, violet the least
strings.b-33.options.1: Violet bends the most, red the least
strings.b-33.options.2: All colours bend by the same angle
strings.b-33.options.3: Green bends the most, orange the least
strings.b-33.explanation: Different colours bend through different angles as they pass through the prism. Red light bends the least and violet the most, which is why the colours come out along separate paths and form a spectrum.
strings.b-34.paragraphs.0: You may have seen objects wavering or flickering when you look at them through the hot air rising above a fire or a radiator. The air just above the fire is hotter than the air further up.
strings.b-34.paragraphs.1: Hotter air is lighter, that is, less dense, than the cooler air above it, and its refractive index is slightly less than that of the cooler air. Since the physical conditions of the air are not stationary, the apparent position of the object seen through the hot air keeps fluctuating. This is atmospheric refraction on a small scale in our local environment.
strings.b-34.paragraphs.2: The twinkling of stars is a similar phenomenon on a much larger scale. Starlight, on entering the earth's atmosphere, undergoes refraction continuously before it reaches the earth. The atmosphere bends starlight towards the normal, so the apparent position of the star is slightly different from its actual position.
strings.b-34.paragraphs.3: A star near the horizon appears slightly higher than its actual position. Its apparent position is not stationary but keeps changing slightly, because the physical conditions of the atmosphere are not stationary. As the path of the light rays keeps varying, the apparent position of the star fluctuates and the amount of starlight entering the eye flickers, so the star sometimes appears brighter and at other times fainter. That is the twinkling effect.
strings.b-35.paragraphs.0: The planets do not twinkle. They are much closer to the earth and are seen as extended sources. If we think of a planet as a collection of a large number of point-sized sources of light, the total variation in the amount of light entering our eye from all those sources averages out to zero, which nullifies the twinkling effect.
strings.b-35.paragraphs.1: Because of atmospheric refraction, the Sun is visible to us about 2 minutes before the actual sunrise and about 2 minutes after the actual sunset. By actual sunrise we mean the actual crossing of the horizon by the Sun.
strings.b-35.paragraphs.2: The apparent flattening of the Sun's disc at sunrise and sunset is also due to the same phenomenon.
strings.b-36.caption: Apparent star position due to atmospheric refraction. The starlight bends as it passes through the atmosphere and reaches the eye, so the star appears along the dashed line, at a position slightly higher than its actual position.
strings.b-37.question: Why do stars twinkle?
strings.b-37.options.0: Because stars change their brightness on their own
strings.b-37.options.1: Because of atmospheric refraction of starlight that keeps changing
strings.b-37.options.2: Because stars move very rapidly across the sky
strings.b-37.explanation: The atmosphere bends starlight towards the normal, so the apparent position of the star differs from its actual position. Since the physical conditions of the atmosphere are not stationary, the apparent position keeps fluctuating, the amount of starlight entering the eye flickers, and the star seems to twinkle.
strings.b-38.question: Why do the planets not twinkle?
strings.b-38.options.0: They are much closer and are seen as extended sources, so the variations average out to zero
strings.b-38.options.1: They do not emit any light of their own
strings.b-38.options.2: They are too far away to be seen clearly
strings.b-38.options.3: Their light does not enter the earth's atmosphere
strings.b-38.explanation: A planet is much closer to the earth than a star and is seen as an extended source. Treating it as a large collection of point-sized sources, the total variation in light from all of them averages out to zero, which nullifies the twinkling effect.
strings.b-39.paragraphs.0: The path of a beam of light passing through a true solution is not visible. It becomes visible when it passes through a colloidal solution, where the size of the particles is relatively larger.
strings.b-39.paragraphs.1: The earth's atmosphere is a heterogeneous mixture of minute particles: smoke, tiny water droplets, suspended particles of dust and molecules of air. When a beam of light strikes such fine particles, the path of the beam becomes visible, because the light reaches us after being reflected diffusely by these particles. This scattering of light by colloidal particles gives rise to the Tyndall effect.
strings.b-39.paragraphs.2: The Tyndall effect is seen when a fine beam of sunlight enters a smoke-filled room through a small hole, and also when sunlight passes through the canopy of a dense forest, where tiny water droplets in the mist scatter the light.
strings.b-39.paragraphs.3: The colour of the scattered light depends on the size of the scattering particles. Very fine particles scatter mainly blue light, while particles of larger size scatter light of longer wavelengths. If the particles are large enough, the scattered light may even appear white.
strings.b-40.paragraphs.0: The molecules of air and other fine particles in the atmosphere are smaller than the wavelength of visible light. They are more effective in scattering light of shorter wavelengths at the blue end than light of longer wavelengths at the red end.
strings.b-40.paragraphs.1: Red light has a wavelength about 1.8 times greater than blue light. So when sunlight passes through the atmosphere, the fine particles in the air scatter the blue colour more strongly than the red, and the scattered blue light enters our eyes.
strings.b-40.paragraphs.2: If the earth had no atmosphere there would be no scattering at all, and the sky would look dark. That is why the sky appears dark to passengers flying at very high altitudes, where scattering is not prominent.
strings.b-40.paragraphs.3: You may have noticed that danger signal lights are red. Red is the least scattered by fog or smoke, so a red light can be seen in the same colour from a distance.
strings.b-41.question: Why does the sky appear dark instead of blue to an astronaut?
strings.b-41.options.0: There is no atmosphere at that height, so there is no scattering
strings.b-41.options.1: The Sun's light is too weak up there
strings.b-41.options.2: The astronaut's eyes cannot detect the colour blue
strings.b-41.options.3: The atmosphere is thicker at that height
strings.b-41.explanation: The blue colour of the sky comes from the scattering of sunlight by fine particles in the atmosphere. With no atmosphere there is no scattering, so the sky looks dark. For the same reason the sky appears dark to passengers flying at very high altitudes.
strings.b-42.paragraphs.0: Our eyes can live even after our death. By donating our eyes after we die, we can light the life of a blind person.
strings.b-42.paragraphs.1: About 35 million people in the developing world are blind, and most of them can be cured. About 4.5 million people with corneal blindness can be cured through corneal transplantation of donated eyes, and 60% of them are children below the age of 12.
strings.b-42.paragraphs.2: Eye donors can belong to any age group or sex. People who use spectacles, or who have been operated on for cataract, can still donate their eyes.
strings.b-42.paragraphs.3: Eyes must be removed within 4-6 hours after death, and the nearest eye bank should be informed immediately. Eye removal takes only 10-15 minutes and does not lead to any disfigurement. One pair of eyes gives vision to up to four corneal blind people.
strings.b-43.question: One pair of donated eyes can give vision to how many corneal blind people?
strings.b-43.explanation: One pair of eyes gives vision to up to four corneal blind people. Eyes must be removed within 4-6 hours after death, and people who use spectacles or have been operated on for cataract can still donate their eyes.

lesson.title: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
objectives: After this lesson you can describe the parts of the human eye and explain what each part does as light travels into it.
After this lesson you can explain accommodation and state the near point and the far point of a normal eye.
After this lesson you can identify myopia, hypermetropia and presbyopia and say which lens corrects each defect.
After this lesson you can explain refraction through a prism, dispersion and the rainbow, why stars twinkle, and why the sky is blue.

sections.title: The human eye
paragraphs: Of all our sense organs, the eye is the one that lets us see the world and its colours. Close your eyes and you can still recognise many things by smell, taste, sound or touch, but you cannot tell what colour anything is.
The human eye works very much like a camera. Its lens system forms an image on a light-sensitive screen inside the eye, and that screen is a membrane called the retina.

The eyeball is roughly spherical, with a diameter of about 2.3 cm. Light enters it through a thin membrane at the front called the cornea, which forms a transparent bulge on the front surface of the eyeball.

Most of the refraction of the light entering the eye happens at the outer surface of the cornea. The crystalline lens inside the eye only makes the finer adjustment of focal length needed to focus objects at different distances on the retina.
Behind the cornea sits the iris, a dark muscular diaphragm. It controls the size of the pupil, the opening at its centre, and the pupil regulates and controls the amount of light entering the eye.
At the back of the eye, the retina is a delicate membrane packed with an enormous number of light-sensitive cells. When light falls on them they get activated and generate electrical signals.
These signals travel along the optic nerves to the brain. The brain interprets them and processes the information, so that we perceive objects as they are.
The eye lens forms an inverted real image of the object on the retina. It is the brain that makes sense of this image for us.

sections.title: Power of accommodation, near point and far point
paragraphs: The eye lens is made of a fibrous, jelly-like material. Its curvature can be changed to some extent by the ciliary muscles, and changing the curvature changes the focal length of the lens.
When the ciliary muscles are relaxed, the lens becomes thin. Its focal length increases, and this lets us see distant objects clearly.

When you look at an object closer to the eye, the ciliary muscles contract. The curvature of the eye lens increases, the lens becomes thicker, and its focal length decreases. This lets us see nearby objects clearly.
The ability of the eye lens to adjust its focal length is called accommodation.

There is a limit to this. The focal length of the eye lens cannot be decreased below a certain minimum. Try reading a printed page held very close to your eyes: the image blurs and the eye feels strained.

To see an object comfortably and distinctly, hold it about 25 cm from the eyes. The minimum distance at which objects can be seen most distinctly without strain is called the least distance of distinct vision, or the near point of the eye. For a young adult with normal vision the near point is about 25 cm.

The farthest point up to which the eye can see objects clearly is called the far point of the eye. For a normal eye the far point is infinity. So a normal eye can see clearly objects that are anywhere between 25 cm and infinity.

Sometimes the crystalline lens of people at old age becomes milky and cloudy. This condition is called cataract. It causes partial or complete loss of vision, and vision can be restored through a cataract surgery.

sections.title: Defects of vision and their correction
paragraphs: Sometimes the eye gradually loses its power of accommodation. The person then cannot see objects distinctly and comfortably, and vision becomes blurred because of refractive defects of the eye.
There are mainly three common refractive defects of vision: myopia or near-sightedness, hypermetropia or far-sightedness, and presbyopia. They can be corrected by using suitable spherical lenses.

Myopia is also known as near-sightedness. A person with myopia can see nearby objects clearly but cannot see distant objects distinctly. The far point of such a person is nearer than infinity; the person may see clearly only up to a distance of a few metres.

In a myopic eye, the image of a distant object is formed in front of the retina and not at the retina itself. This defect may arise because of excessive curvature of the eye lens, or because the eyeball has become elongated.
Myopia is corrected by using a concave lens of suitable power. The concave lens brings the image back on to the retina.

Hypermetropia is also known as far-sightedness. A person with hypermetropia can see distant objects clearly but cannot see nearby objects distinctly. The near point of such a person is farther away than the normal 25 cm, so the person has to keep reading material much beyond 25 cm from the eye.

This happens because light rays from a close by object are focussed at a point behind the retina. The defect arises either because the focal length of the eye lens is too long, or because the eyeball has become too small.
Hypermetropia is corrected by using a convex lens of appropriate power. Eye-glasses with converging lenses provide the additional focussing power needed to form the image on the retina.

The power of accommodation of the eye usually decreases with ageing, and the near point gradually recedes. People then find it difficult to see nearby objects comfortably and distinctly without corrective eye-glasses. This defect is called presbyopia. It arises due to the gradual weakening of the ciliary muscles and diminishing flexibility of the eye lens.

Sometimes a person may suffer from both myopia and hypermetropia. Such people often require bi-focal lenses, which consist of both concave and convex lenses: the upper portion is a concave lens for distant vision, and the lower part is a convex lens for near vision.
These days refractive defects can also be corrected with contact lenses or through surgical interventions.

sections.title: Refraction of light through a prism
paragraphs: Light passing through a rectangular glass slab comes out parallel to the direction in which it entered, only slightly displaced sideways, because the slab's two refracting surfaces are parallel.

A triangular glass prism is different. It has two triangular bases and three rectangular lateral surfaces, and these surfaces are inclined to each other. The angle between its two lateral faces is called the angle of the prism.

When a ray of light PE falls on one refracting face of the prism, it bends towards the normal as it enters the glass and travels inside as the refracted ray EF. At the second face it passes from glass to air, so it bends away from the normal and leaves as the emergent ray FS.
The peculiar shape of the prism makes the emergent ray bend at an angle to the direction of the incident ray. This angle is called the angle of deviation.

sections.title: Dispersion of white light and the rainbow
paragraphs: When a narrow beam of white light from the Sun is allowed to fall on a glass prism and the emerging light is caught on a nearby screen, a beautiful band of colours appears. The prism has split the white light into a band of colours.
The colours you see, in order, are violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red. The acronym VIBGYOR helps you remember the sequence.
The band of the coloured components of a light beam is called its spectrum. The splitting of light into its component colours is called dispersion.

Why do we get these colours? Different colours of light bend through different angles with respect to the incident ray as they pass through a prism. Red light bends the least and violet bends the most. So the rays of each colour emerge along different paths and become distinct.

Isaac Newton was the first to use a glass prism to obtain the spectrum of sunlight. When he tried to split the colours further with another similar prism, he could not get any more colours. When he placed a second identical prism in an inverted position, all the colours passed through it and a beam of white light emerged on the other side. This gave Newton the idea that sunlight is made up of seven colours.
Any light that gives a spectrum similar to that of sunlight is often referred to as white light.

A rainbow is a natural spectrum appearing in the sky after a rain shower. It is caused by dispersion of sunlight by the tiny water droplets present in the atmosphere. A rainbow is always formed in a direction opposite to that of the Sun.

The water droplets act like small prisms. They refract and disperse the incident sunlight, then reflect it internally, and finally refract it again as it comes out of the raindrop. Because of this dispersion and internal reflection, different colours reach the observer's eye.
You can also see a rainbow on a sunny day by looking at the sky through a waterfall or a water fountain with the Sun behind you.

sections.title: Atmospheric refraction
paragraphs: You may have seen objects wavering or flickering when you look at them through the hot air rising above a fire or a radiator. The air just above the fire is hotter than the air further up.

Hotter air is lighter, that is, less dense, than the cooler air above it, and its refractive index is slightly less than that of the cooler air. Since the physical conditions of the air are not stationary, the apparent position of the object seen through the hot air keeps fluctuating. This is atmospheric refraction on a small scale in our local environment.

The twinkling of stars is a similar phenomenon on a much larger scale. Starlight, on entering the earth's atmosphere, undergoes refraction continuously before it reaches the earth. The atmosphere bends starlight towards the normal, so the apparent position of the star is slightly different from its actual position.

A star near the horizon appears slightly higher than its actual position. Its apparent position is not stationary but keeps changing slightly, because the physical conditions of the atmosphere are not stationary. As the path of the light rays keeps varying, the apparent position of the star fluctuates and the amount of starlight entering the eye flickers, so the star sometimes appears brighter and at other times fainter. That is the twinkling effect.

The planets do not twinkle. They are much closer to the earth and are seen as extended sources. If we think of a planet as a collection of a large number of point-sized sources of light, the total variation in the amount of light entering our eye from all those sources averages out to zero, which nullifies the twinkling effect.

Because of atmospheric refraction, the Sun is visible to us about 2 minutes before the actual sunrise and about 2 minutes after the actual sunset. By actual sunrise we mean the actual crossing of the horizon by the Sun.
The apparent flattening of the Sun's disc at sunrise and sunset is also due to the same phenomenon.

sections.title: Scattering of light
paragraphs: The interplay of light with objects around us gives rise to many spectacular phenomena: the blue colour of the sky, the colour of water in the deep sea, and the reddening of the Sun at sunrise and sunset.
The path of a beam of light passing through a true solution is not visible. It becomes visible when it passes through a colloidal solution, where the size of the particles is relatively larger.

The earth's atmosphere is a heterogeneous mixture of minute particles: smoke, tiny water droplets, suspended particles of dust and molecules of air. When a beam of light strikes such fine particles, the path of the beam becomes visible, because the light reaches us after being reflected diffusely by these particles. This scattering of light by colloidal particles gives rise to the Tyndall effect.

The Tyndall effect is seen when a fine beam of sunlight enters a smoke-filled room through a small hole, and also when sunlight passes through the canopy of a dense forest, where tiny water droplets in the mist scatter the light.

The colour of the scattered light depends on the size of the scattering particles. Very fine particles scatter mainly blue light, while particles of larger size scatter light of longer wavelengths. If the particles are large enough, the scattered light may even appear white.

The molecules of air and other fine particles in the atmosphere are smaller than the wavelength of visible light. They are more effective in scattering light of shorter wavelengths at the blue end than light of longer wavelengths at the red end.

Red light has a wavelength about 1.8 times greater than blue light. So when sunlight passes through the atmosphere, the fine particles in the air scatter the blue colour more strongly than the red, and the scattered blue light enters our eyes.

If the earth had no atmosphere there would be no scattering at all, and the sky would look dark. That is why the sky appears dark to passengers flying at very high altitudes, where scattering is not prominent.
You may have noticed that danger signal lights are red. Red is the least scattered by fog or smoke, so a red light can be seen in the same colour from a distance.

sections.title: Eye donation
paragraphs: Our eyes can live even after our death. By donating our eyes after we die, we can light the life of a blind person.

About 35 million people in the developing world are blind, and most of them can be cured. About 4.5 million people with corneal blindness can be cured through corneal transplantation of donated eyes, and 60% of them are children below the age of 12.
Eye donors can belong to any age group or sex. People who use spectacles, or who have been operated on for cataract, can still donate their eyes.

Eyes must be removed within 4-6 hours after death, and the nearest eye bank should be informed immediately. Eye removal takes only 10-15 minutes and does not lead to any disfigurement. One pair of eyes gives vision to up to four corneal blind people.

options: The ability of the eye to change the size of its pupil
The ability of the eye lens to adjust its focal length
The ability of the retina to change its sensitivity
The ability of the eye to move inside its socket

spec.question: The human eye can focus on objects at different distances by adjusting the focal length of the eye lens. This is due to
spec.answer: accommodation
spec.explanation: Adjusting the focal length of the eye lens is exactly what accommodation means. Presbyopia, myopia and hypermetropia are defects, not the normal ability.
spec.expected_understanding: The student can separate the normal power of accommodation from the defects of vision.

spec.question: The change in focal length of an eye lens is caused by the action of the
spec.answer: ciliary muscles
spec.explanation: The ciliary muscles change the curvature of the eye lens. More curvature means a thicker lens and a shorter focal length; relaxed muscles mean a thin lens and a longer focal length.
spec.expected_understanding: The student links the ciliary muscles to the change of curvature and focal length.

spec.answer: 25 cm

spec.expected_understanding: The student remembers the standard value 25 cm with the correct unit.

spec.question: What are the far point and the near point of a human eye with normal vision?
options: Far point 25 cm, near point infinity
Far point infinity, near point 25 cm
Far point 2.5 cm, near point infinity
Far point infinity, near point 2.3 cm
spec.answer: Far point infinity, near point 25 cm
spec.explanation: For a normal eye the far point is infinity and the near point is about 25 cm, so the eye can see clearly anything between 25 cm and infinity.
spec.expected_understanding: The student keeps the two standard points the right way round.

spec.question: Why is a normal eye not able to see clearly the objects placed closer than 25 cm?
options: The pupil cannot open wide enough
The focal length of the eye lens cannot be decreased below a certain minimum limit
The retina stops sending electrical signals
The iris blocks the light completely
spec.answer: The focal length of the eye lens cannot be decreased below a certain minimum limit
spec.explanation: The ciliary muscles can increase the curvature of the eye lens only up to a point, so the focal length cannot be reduced below a minimum. Objects closer than about 25 cm therefore give a blurred image and strain the eye.
spec.expected_understanding: The student connects the 25 cm limit to the minimum possible focal length of the eye lens.

spec.question: What happens to the image distance in the eye when we increase the distance of an object from the eye?
options: It stays the same, because the image is always formed on the retina
spec.answer: It stays the same, because the image is always formed on the retina
spec.explanation: The retina is fixed at the back of the eye, so the image must always fall on it. When the object moves farther away, the eye does not move the image; instead the ciliary muscles change the curvature of the eye lens and hence its focal length, so that the image still lands on the retina.
spec.expected_understanding: The student sees accommodation as a change of focal length, not a change of image position.

paragraphs: The power of accommodation of the eye usually decreases with ageing, and the near point gradually recedes. People then find it difficult to see nearby objects comfortably and distinctly without corrective eye-glasses. This defect is called presbyopia. It arises due to the gradual weakening of the ciliary muscles and diminishing flexibility of the eye lens.

Sometimes a person may suffer from both myopia and hypermetropia. Such people often require bi-focal lenses, which consist of both concave and convex lenses: the upper portion is a concave lens for distant vision, and the lower part is a convex lens for near vision.
These days refractive defects can also be corrected with contact lenses or through surgical interventions.

spec.question: A person with a myopic eye cannot see objects beyond 1.2 m distinctly. What should be the type of the corrective lens used to restore proper vision?
spec.answer: a concave lens
spec.explanation: Myopia is corrected by a concave lens of suitable power. The person's far point is only 1.2 m, so the concave lens must bring the image of a distant object back from in front of the retina on to the retina.
spec.expected_understanding: The student matches myopia with a concave lens and does not confuse it with hypermetropia.

spec.question: A student has difficulty reading the blackboard while sitting in the last row. What could be the defect the child is suffering from, and how can it be corrected?
options: Hypermetropia, corrected by a convex lens
Myopia, corrected by a concave lens
Presbyopia, corrected by a bi-focal lens
spec.answer: Myopia, corrected by a concave lens
spec.explanation: The blackboard is far away, and a child who cannot read it from the last row cannot see distant objects distinctly. That is myopia, and it is corrected with a concave lens of suitable power.
spec.expected_understanding: The student can diagnose a defect from a described everyday situation.

steps.title: Power is measured in dioptres
steps.detail: Lens power is quoted in dioptres, written D. The numerical problems in this chapter use values such as -5.5 D for distant vision and +1.5 D for near vision.

steps.title: Power and focal length
steps.detail: The power P of a lens and its focal length f in metres are related by P = 1/f, so f = 1/P. Work with f in metres and the power comes out in dioptres.

steps.title: The sign of the power tells you which lens
steps.detail: The lens used to correct myopia, which is a concave lens, is the one the chapter quotes with a minus sign (-5.5 D). The lens used to correct hypermetropia, which is a convex lens, is the one quoted with a plus sign (+1.5 D).

spec.problem: A person needs a lens of power -5.5 dioptres for correcting his distant vision. For correcting his near vision he needs a lens of power +1.5 dioptre. What is the focal length of the lens required for correcting (i) distant vision, and (ii) near vision?

steps.title: Write down what is given
steps.detail: Power of the lens for distant vision P = -5.5 D. Power of the lens for near vision P = +1.5 D.

steps.title: Choose the relation
steps.detail: Power and focal length are related by P = 1/f with f in metres, so f = 1/P. The answer comes out in metres.

steps.title: Distant vision
steps.detail: f = 1/(-5.5) = -0.18 m, that is about -18 cm. The negative sign shows it is a concave lens.

steps.title: Near vision
steps.detail: f = 1/(+1.5) = +0.67 m, that is about +67 cm. The positive sign shows it is a convex lens.

spec.answer: Distant vision: focal length about -0.18 m (about -18 cm), a concave lens. Near vision: focal length about +0.67 m (about +67 cm), a convex lens.

spec.problem: The far point of a myopic person is 80 cm in front of the eye. What is the nature and power of the lens required to correct the problem?

steps.title: What the lens has to do
steps.detail: The person must be able to see distant objects clearly. The corrective lens must therefore form the image of a very distant object at the person's own far point, 80 cm in front of the eye.

steps.title: Focal length of the required lens
steps.detail: For an object at infinity the image forms at the focal point of the lens, so the focal length must be 80 cm: f = -80 cm = -0.8 m. The minus sign is used because this image is on the same side of the lens as the object.

steps.title: Nature of the lens
steps.detail: A negative power means a concave lens, which is exactly what myopia needs.

spec.answer: A concave lens of power -1.25 D.

spec.problem: Make a diagram to show how hypermetropia is corrected. The near point of a hypermetropic eye is 1 m. What is the power of the lens required to correct this defect? Assume that the near point of the normal eye is 25 cm.

steps.title: What the lens has to do
steps.detail: The person must be able to read at the normal near point of 25 cm. So an object placed at 25 cm must produce an image at the person's own near point, 1 m, on the same side of the lens.

steps.title: Object distance
steps.detail: u = -25 cm = -0.25 m. The object is on the near side of the lens, so its distance is taken as negative.

steps.title: Image distance
steps.detail: v = -1 m. The image is virtual and on the same side as the object, so it is also negative.

steps.title: Focal length and power
steps.detail: f = 1/3 m = +0.33 m, and P = 1/f = +3.0 D. The positive sign tells us the lens is convex.

spec.answer: A convex lens of power +3.0 D (focal length about +0.33 m). The ray diagram is the one shown in the figure above: the convex lens makes the rays from the object at 25 cm meet on the retina.

paragraphs: Light passing through a rectangular glass slab comes out parallel to the direction in which it entered, only slightly displaced sideways, because the slab's two refracting surfaces are parallel.

A triangular glass prism is different. It has two triangular bases and three rectangular lateral surfaces, and these surfaces are inclined to each other. The angle between its two lateral faces is called the angle of the prism.

When a ray of light PE falls on one refracting face of the prism, it bends towards the normal as it enters the glass and travels inside as the refracted ray EF. At the second face it passes from glass to air, so it bends away from the normal and leaves as the emergent ray FS.
The peculiar shape of the prism makes the emergent ray bend at an angle to the direction of the incident ray. This angle is called the angle of deviation.

spec.question: In a triangular glass prism, the angle between its two lateral faces is called
spec.answer: the angle of the prism
spec.explanation: A triangular prism has two triangular bases and three rectangular lateral surfaces. The angle between its two lateral faces is the angle of the prism, marked A in the ray diagram.
spec.expected_understanding: The student can name the angles of a prism correctly.

paragraphs: When a narrow beam of white light from the Sun is allowed to fall on a glass prism and the emerging light is caught on a nearby screen, a beautiful band of colours appears. The prism has split the white light into a band of colours.
The colours you see, in order, are violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red. The acronym VIBGYOR helps you remember the sequence.
The band of the coloured components of a light beam is called its spectrum. The splitting of light into its component colours is called dispersion.

Why do we get these colours? Different colours of light bend through different angles with respect to the incident ray as they pass through a prism. Red light bends the least and violet bends the most. So the rays of each colour emerge along different paths and become distinct.

paragraphs: Isaac Newton was the first to use a glass prism to obtain the spectrum of sunlight. When he tried to split the colours further with another similar prism, he could not get any more colours. When he placed a second identical prism in an inverted position, all the colours passed through it and a beam of white light emerged on the other side. This gave Newton the idea that sunlight is made up of seven colours.
Any light that gives a spectrum similar to that of sunlight is often referred to as white light.

A rainbow is a natural spectrum appearing in the sky after a rain shower. It is caused by dispersion of sunlight by the tiny water droplets present in the atmosphere. A rainbow is always formed in a direction opposite to that of the Sun.

The water droplets act like small prisms. They refract and disperse the incident sunlight, then reflect it internally, and finally refract it again as it comes out of the raindrop. Because of this dispersion and internal reflection, different colours reach the observer's eye.
You can also see a rainbow on a sunny day by looking at the sky through a waterfall or a water fountain with the Sun behind you.

spec.question: When white light passes through a glass prism, which colour bends the most and which the least?
options: Red bends the most, violet the least
Violet bends the most, red the least
All colours bend by the same angle
Green bends the most, orange the least
spec.answer: Violet bends the most, red the least
spec.explanation: Different colours bend through different angles as they pass through the prism. Red light bends the least and violet the most, which is why the colours come out along separate paths and form a spectrum.
spec.expected_understanding: The student knows why the colours separate instead of staying together.

paragraphs: You may have seen objects wavering or flickering when you look at them through the hot air rising above a fire or a radiator. The air just above the fire is hotter than the air further up.

Hotter air is lighter, that is, less dense, than the cooler air above it, and its refractive index is slightly less than that of the cooler air. Since the physical conditions of the air are not stationary, the apparent position of the object seen through the hot air keeps fluctuating. This is atmospheric refraction on a small scale in our local environment.

The twinkling of stars is a similar phenomenon on a much larger scale. Starlight, on entering the earth's atmosphere, undergoes refraction continuously before it reaches the earth. The atmosphere bends starlight towards the normal, so the apparent position of the star is slightly different from its actual position.

A star near the horizon appears slightly higher than its actual position. Its apparent position is not stationary but keeps changing slightly, because the physical conditions of the atmosphere are not stationary. As the path of the light rays keeps varying, the apparent position of the star fluctuates and the amount of starlight entering the eye flickers, so the star sometimes appears brighter and at other times fainter. That is the twinkling effect.

The planets do not twinkle. They are much closer to the earth and are seen as extended sources. If we think of a planet as a collection of a large number of point-sized sources of light, the total variation in the amount of light entering our eye from all those sources averages out to zero, which nullifies the twinkling effect.

Because of atmospheric refraction, the Sun is visible to us about 2 minutes before the actual sunrise and about 2 minutes after the actual sunset. By actual sunrise we mean the actual crossing of the horizon by the Sun.
The apparent flattening of the Sun's disc at sunrise and sunset is also due to the same phenomenon.

spec.question: Why do stars twinkle?
options: Because stars change their brightness on their own
Because of atmospheric refraction of starlight that keeps changing
Because stars move very rapidly across the sky
spec.answer: Because of atmospheric refraction of starlight that keeps changing
spec.explanation: The atmosphere bends starlight towards the normal, so the apparent position of the star differs from its actual position. Since the physical conditions of the atmosphere are not stationary, the apparent position keeps fluctuating, the amount of starlight entering the eye flickers, and the star seems to twinkle.
spec.expected_understanding: The student explains twinkling through refraction in a medium of gradually changing refractive index.

spec.question: Why do the planets not twinkle?
options: They are much closer and are seen as extended sources, so the variations average out to zero
They do not emit any light of their own
They are too far away to be seen clearly
Their light does not enter the earth's atmosphere
spec.answer: They are much closer and are seen as extended sources, so the variations average out to zero
spec.explanation: A planet is much closer to the earth than a star and is seen as an extended source. Treating it as a large collection of point-sized sources, the total variation in light from all of them averages out to zero, which nullifies the twinkling effect.
spec.expected_understanding: The student contrasts a point source with an extended source to explain the difference.

paragraphs: The path of a beam of light passing through a true solution is not visible. It becomes visible when it passes through a colloidal solution, where the size of the particles is relatively larger.

The earth's atmosphere is a heterogeneous mixture of minute particles: smoke, tiny water droplets, suspended particles of dust and molecules of air. When a beam of light strikes such fine particles, the path of the beam becomes visible, because the light reaches us after being reflected diffusely by these particles. This scattering of light by colloidal particles gives rise to the Tyndall effect.

The Tyndall effect is seen when a fine beam of sunlight enters a smoke-filled room through a small hole, and also when sunlight passes through the canopy of a dense forest, where tiny water droplets in the mist scatter the light.

The colour of the scattered light depends on the size of the scattering particles. Very fine particles scatter mainly blue light, while particles of larger size scatter light of longer wavelengths. If the particles are large enough, the scattered light may even appear white.

The molecules of air and other fine particles in the atmosphere are smaller than the wavelength of visible light. They are more effective in scattering light of shorter wavelengths at the blue end than light of longer wavelengths at the red end.

Red light has a wavelength about 1.8 times greater than blue light. So when sunlight passes through the atmosphere, the fine particles in the air scatter the blue colour more strongly than the red, and the scattered blue light enters our eyes.

If the earth had no atmosphere there would be no scattering at all, and the sky would look dark. That is why the sky appears dark to passengers flying at very high altitudes, where scattering is not prominent.
You may have noticed that danger signal lights are red. Red is the least scattered by fog or smoke, so a red light can be seen in the same colour from a distance.

spec.question: Why does the sky appear dark instead of blue to an astronaut?
options: There is no atmosphere at that height, so there is no scattering
The Sun's light is too weak up there
The astronaut's eyes cannot detect the colour blue
The atmosphere is thicker at that height
spec.answer: There is no atmosphere at that height, so there is no scattering
spec.explanation: The blue colour of the sky comes from the scattering of sunlight by fine particles in the atmosphere. With no atmosphere there is no scattering, so the sky looks dark. For the same reason the sky appears dark to passengers flying at very high altitudes.
spec.expected_understanding: The student links the blue sky directly to scattering by the atmosphere.

paragraphs: Our eyes can live even after our death. By donating our eyes after we die, we can light the life of a blind person.

About 35 million people in the developing world are blind, and most of them can be cured. About 4.5 million people with corneal blindness can be cured through corneal transplantation of donated eyes, and 60% of them are children below the age of 12.
Eye donors can belong to any age group or sex. People who use spectacles, or who have been operated on for cataract, can still donate their eyes.

Eyes must be removed within 4-6 hours after death, and the nearest eye bank should be informed immediately. Eye removal takes only 10-15 minutes and does not lead to any disfigurement. One pair of eyes gives vision to up to four corneal blind people.

spec.question: One pair of donated eyes can give vision to how many corneal blind people?
spec.answer: four
spec.explanation: One pair of eyes gives vision to up to four corneal blind people. Eyes must be removed within 4-6 hours after death, and people who use spectacles or have been operated on for cataract can still donate their eyes.
spec.expected_understanding: The student knows the basic facts about eye donation given in the chapter.
